idiom_name: value semantics + defensive copies + copy-on-write snapshots in atomic.Pointer
implementation_notes: Go has no immutable aggregates and const covers only compile-time constants, so the no-mutation guarantee is a hand-written convention: pass structs and slices by value, return copies (slices.Clone, maps.Clone, append([]T(nil), xs...)) instead of handing out internal state, keep fields unexported with accessor methods, and expose WithX methods that build a new value. For data shared with readers across goroutines, keep a pointer to a fully built value in atomic.Pointer[T]: readers Load a consistent version, writers derive the next one from the old one and Store it - copy-on-write plus atomic publication. What replaces the classic immutable object is therefore ownership discipline and copies, not a type. The explicit structure is still justified for package-level API values, where a constructor plus copy helpers make the convention visible; for a value confined to one goroutine, mutate it directly - Go idiom is to hand ownership over or communicate, not to version everything.
pitfalls: append can write into a shared backing array when capacity allows: b := append(a[:2], x) overwrites a[2]; clone first or use a full slice expression.
Copying is shallow: a struct copy still shares the slice or map it points to, and copying a struct that contains a sync.Mutex trips go vet copylocks.
atomic.Pointer[T] only works if the pointed-to value is never mutated after Store; one in-place field write makes readers race with the writer.
Returning a map or slice field directly hands every caller a mutable alias; document ownership or return a clone at the boundary.
